activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Leave No Trace outdoor ethics are organized as seven principles, including 'dispose of waste properly' and 'leave what you find'.
story:
The boarding call for Denver wasn't for another forty minutes, but Dylan's mother kept checking the gate screen anyway, so Dylan had time to sit with his backpack in his lap and think about the rock.

It was in the front pocket, wrapped in a sock. Rose-colored, flecked with something that caught the light, about the size of a plum. He'd found it last summer on the trail above the lake, when his family had come west before, and he'd slipped it into his pocket without saying anything. His sister had seen him do it. She was younger, but she'd gone quiet on the whole hike home, and for a year Dylan had assumed she was just being annoying. Now he wasn't so sure. This morning at breakfast she'd gone quiet again the moment he mentioned this trip, the same exact silence, the two mornings sitting in his memory like parallel lines, and that pattern made him think the silence had a cause he hadn't looked for. Something to do with the rock.

He pulled out his phone and texted Noam, who had gone to a different park with his uncle in the spring. Noam had talked about it for a week afterward.

Noam's reply came fast, as if he'd been waiting. "You mean you took a rock OUT of a park? That's against the rules. My uncle made me memorize them. Leave No Trace. It's seven principles. Like 'dispose of waste properly.' And 'leave what you find.'"

Dylan read the message twice. Leave what you find. He unzipped the pocket and looked at the rock, and the guilt he'd been carrying around without naming it suddenly had a name. He typed: "What if you already took it? A year ago?"

"Then you take it back," Noam wrote. "Uncle says that's the fix."

Dylan looked at the gate screen. Twenty-five minutes. They were flying to Denver and then driving north, and if he checked the map right, the drive passed within an hour of the same lake. It could work. He turned to his sister, who was slouched beside their mother with her headphones half on.

"Hey," he said. "You remember that rock I took? From the lake trail?"

She pulled one headphone off. Her eyes went straight to his backpack, which told him everything. She had known all along. "You still have it?"

"Yeah. And I'm taking it back. On this trip. Putting it back where I found it."

She studied him for a long moment, the way she did when deciding whether a promise was real. "The exact spot," she said finally. "Not just anywhere."

"The exact spot."

The gate agent picked up the microphone, and Dylan zipped the pocket shut, stood up, and held his backpack against his chest with both hands.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The equality rights in section 15 of the Canadian Charter came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws.
story:
Willow spread the photocopy of the Canadian Charter across the kitchen table and weighted the corners with mugs. The assignment from Mr. Grant was due tomorrow: pick one right, explain it in your own words, and be ready to say something true about it that nobody else in the class would know. Her eyes kept snagging on the small print under section 15, the equality rights. Every other section had the same start date, 1982. Section 15 said 1985.

"That's a misprint," her mother said, passing through with laundry. "Photocopies always mangle something."

Willow didn't think so. The date was printed cleanly, and it appeared twice, in both the English and French columns. A misprint wouldn't be that consistent. She grabbed her phone and called Janelle.

"Drop everything," Janelle said before Willow spoke. "I'm making a poster about freedom of expression and I need it to look eloquent. Like, judges-quoting-me eloquent."

"Janelle. Why would one part of the Charter start three years later than the rest?"

"Three years? That's weird. That's like everybody's birthday except yours showing up late."

Willow frowned at the page. Janelle's joke wasn't a joke, actually. The rest of the Charter had come into force in 1982, and section 15 waited until 1985. That gap had to mean something. She thought of her science class, where you tested an idea by changing one thing and watching what happened. Her simple test: look up whether other official documents had delayed sections. If section 15 were the only one, the delay was about section 15 itself, not about printing schedules or a lazy clerk.

She typed, read, typed again. The pattern held. Governments had been given time to update their laws before the equality rights took effect. So the delay wasn't an accident; it was deliberate, built into the document.

Her palms began to perspire against the phone. This was the thing nobody else would know. She could stand up in Mr. Grant's class and say it.

"Found something?" Janelle asked.

"The equality rights, section 15. They came into force in 1985, three years after the rest, to give governments time to update their laws."

"Update them for what?"

"That's the part I have to explain in my own words," Willow said. "Mr. Grant wants our own words, not the textbook's." She paused. "Want to hear my try?"

"Only if you listen to my poster after."

"Section 15 means the law has to treat everyone as equal. And the three-year wait means even governments needed practice before they had to prove it."

Janelle was quiet for a second. "Huh. That's actually better than eloquent. That's true."

Willow wrote the sentence at the top of a fresh page. Outside, a delivery truck rattled past, and somewhere down the block a screen door banged twice.

"What's your poster line?" she asked.

Janelle cleared her throat. "I may not agree with your poster, but I will defend to the death my right to make mine."

"That's a famous quote, Janelle."

"It's a famous quote with my name on it now," Janelle said, and Willow laughed so hard she knocked a mug off section 2.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologist Thomas Gordon coined the term 'I-message' in the 1960s: a sentence like 'I felt left out' describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with 'you'.
story:
Aaron sat at the kitchen table with his phone face down beside him, staring at a crumpled napkin where he had written his fourth attempt at a text. Kameron had not spoken to him since Friday, when Aaron had found out about the sleepover he was not invited to, and every draft so far started the same way. "You ditched me." "You left me out on purpose." He crossed them out so hard the pen tore the napkin. None of them would work. He knew that much, even if he could not yet explain why.

While hunting for a clean sheet of paper, he dug through his binder and found a worksheet from Ms. Campbell's class that he had never bothered to evaluate properly, since it had been handed back with a check mark and shoved in the back pocket. On it, in his own handwriting from weeks ago, was a note about a psychologist named Thomas Gordon, who in the 1960s coined the term "I-message": a sentence like "I felt left out" describes the speaker's feelings instead of blaming the listener with "you." Aaron read it twice. So that was why every draft had felt like a thrown rock. He had been aiming every word at Kameron, and a person who feels attacked ducks.

He decided to test the idea, because it seemed almost too simple. He wrote "You ditched me" on one line, then rewrote it underneath as "I felt left out when I heard about the sleepover." He read both aloud to the empty kitchen. The first one put his fists up. The second one, awkward as it sounded, left a door open. There was still the matter of actually sending it, which felt like an obligation he could not shake, so he picked up the phone before he could talk himself out of it.

The reply came while he was pacing the arid, sun-baked back porch, where the potted plant his mom kept forgetting to water had gone crispy at the edges. "Come outside," Kameron wrote. "Backyard. Now."

Kameron was standing by the fence, holding a lopsided posterboard that read HAPPY EARLY BIRTHDAY, with the B drawn backwards. "It was supposed to be a surprise party," he said, ears going red. "That's the sleepover. Wallace was helping me plan it. That's why nobody told you anything."

"You could have just said that," Aaron said, though his voice cracked halfway, which ruined the effect.

"You could have just asked instead of going quiet for three days," Kameron said, and then, quieter, "I got your text. That I-message thing."

"You know about those?"

"Ms. Campbell taught us that in September. You were absent," Kameron said, and grinned. "It's a good one, though. Handmade birthday posters with the wrong date on them, apparently, need a strong opener too."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see.
story:
Alexander had promised Mr. Swampy, the farmer down the road, that he would not set foot in the barn again after the incident with the goat and the feed bucket. That promise was why he was now crouched beside the barn door on a milk crate, holding a microscope Mr. Swampy had lent him, with a fresh onion in his lap.

"You look like a diplomat negotiating a peace treaty with that onion," said Dominique, perched on the fence. Collin sat beside her, unwrapping a sandwich he had clearly brought for moral support.

"I'm being careful. Mr. Swampy prohibits barn entry, not barn-adjacent entry. There's a difference." Alexander peeled a translucent layer from the inside of the onion, the part thin enough to read a newspaper through, and laid a square of it on a slide. His assignment was due Monday: draw the cells and label the cell wall, the membrane, and the nucleus. He'd left it until Sunday, which Dominique had described, twice, as "a choice."

He squinted into the eyepiece. He squinted harder. There was a pale wash of nothing, like looking through a fogged window at an empty parking lot. He turned the focus knob so far that the knob itself seemed embarrassed.

"Cells?" Collin offered.

"Invisible cells. Award-winning invisible cells." Alexander sat back. "Maybe I peeled it wrong. Maybe onions from this farm are secretly ghosts."

Dominique slid off the fence and leaned over the slide. "It's not you. Onion skin cells are nearly colourless, so a drop of iodine stain is often added to make the nucleus and cell wall easier to see. We did it in class Tuesday. Tuesday, when you were drawing a rocket on your worksheet."

"I was labelling the rocket."

"With what?"

"Enthusiasm."

Collin dug in his backpack and produced the little brown dropper bottle from his science kit, which he carried everywhere for reasons no one questioned anymore. Alexander put one careful drop on the skin, pressed down the cover slip, and bent to the eyepiece.

The slide bloomed into a honeycomb, each cell a neat brick in a pale gold wall. He could see the thick outer line of the cell wall, the finer line of the membrane hugging it inside, and, floating near the middle of each cell, a small dark sphere.

"There you are," Alexander said. "Nucleus, cell wall, membrane. All present." He started his drawing, tongue between his teeth.

"Better than the rocket?" Dominique asked.

"The rocket had style. This has structure." He tapped the page. "Whether it's better is subjective, but it's the one getting a grade."

The barn door creaked open behind them. Mr. Swampy stood there, arms crossed, holding a second onion.

"Since you're working," he said, "you might as well know the rest of these need sorting."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: A name a group uses for itself is called an endonym, and a name outsiders use for it is an exonym; Germans call their country Deutschland, while English speakers say Germany.
story:
The poster board had a hole in it where Dereck's elbow had gone through during fourth period, and the heritage fair started in forty minutes. Zachary smoothed tape over the tear and stared at the title, "Where Our Names Come From," which had seemed like a good idea on Monday and now looked like a homework emergency.

The project was supposed to be about the countries on the classroom map, but it had turned into something stranger once he started asking people what they called the places themselves. Avi crouched beside him in the gym, arranging index cards. "You have to fix the Germany card," she said. "You wrote that Germans call their country Germany."

"They do. In English."

"Exactly. That's the whole point of your project, and you got it wrong on the main card."

Zachary flipped through his notes. He remembered the exact moment the project had changed direction, two weeks ago at his grandmother's kitchen table, when his cousin Mira had come to visit from abroad. Someone had asked her what it was like living where she did, using the English name for her country, and she had laughed until she had to put down her tea. "You keep saying it like that," she had said. "We never call it that. Not once, not at home." His uncle had shrugged and said that was just how maps worked, and Mira had said maps were made by people who had never asked.

Back in the gym, Avi was holding up two cards. "So the word you told me yesterday. Say it again, because it's the best part."

"An endonym," Zachary said. "It's what a group calls itself. What outsiders use is an exonym."

"Which one is Germany, then?"

"Exonym. Deutschland is the endonym. Every German says Deutschland, and every English speaker says Germany, and somehow nobody's ever fought about it, which is honestly the strangest part."

Dereck wandered over from the drinks table with a cookie in each hand. He had been assigned the tech corner, where a borrowed motion sensor was supposed to greet visitors with a recorded message whenever anyone walked past. "I can't calibrate this thing," he announced, chewing. "It either stays silent or screams hello at the wall every eight seconds."

Zachary went to look, mostly because the poster board was finished and worrying about it had stopped being productive. The sensor was a gray box duct-taped to a music stand, aimed at the doorway. He turned the sensitivity dial a quarter turn and walked in and out until the recording triggered once per person, which took four tries and one false start in which it greeted a folding chair.

"That actually works," Dereck said, in the tone of someone who had not expected it to work.

By the time Ms. Sato arrived with the visiting parents, the gym smelled like cookies and the display was holding together, hole and all. A small crowd formed at Zachary's table, and a man leaned in to read the Germany card, then read it again. "My grandmother's recipes are from there," he said. "Or from Deutschland, I suppose I should say." He said the second word carefully, like handing back something borrowed.

Ms. Sato stopped at the table last of all. "The tape on the corner is a nice touch," she said. "Very honest."

"It was Dereck's elbow."

"Even better." She picked up the card about endangered languages, the one listing tongues spoken by only a few families left, and read it quietly. Then she set it down and said, "The fair's over in ten minutes. You three should take a cookie before the parents finish them."

The motion sensor said hello to her as she walked away, exactly once, perfectly on time.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: The U.S. agency NIOSH recommends limiting exposure to 85 decibels to eight hours a day, and each 3-decibel increase halves the safe listening time.
story:
Alexandra sat in the back seat of the family car, watching her mom's hands shift on the steering wheel, and tried to remember whether she had actually agreed to this dance or only failed to say no. Noemie had a seat beside her, wearing a dress that corresponded to nothing in Alexandra's own closet, all silver and impossible. Paige was in the front, already arguing about parking. "There's a lot behind the gym," Paige said. "There is never a spot behind the gym," said Alexandra's mom, and turned in anyway.

Last year, at the fall festival, Alexandra had spent the whole evening beside the stage because her friends liked being close to the band, and afterward her ears had rung until midnight. She had thought that was just what concerts did, a price you paid, part of the heritage of loud music the way sticky floors were part of gym dances. She'd mentioned the ringing to Ms. Paquette, her neighbour, who happened to work in hearing safety. "Eighty-five decibels is fine for eight hours," Ms. Paquette had said, "but every 3 decibels louder cuts that safe time in half. Eighty-eight, you get four hours. Ninety-one, two." Alexandra had nodded and forgotten it, mostly.

They found a spot behind the gym, because of course there was one tonight. Inside, the speakers stood taller than the doors, black and stacked, and Noemie headed straight for the wall beneath them like a moth to a porch light. Alexandra followed, but she kept her eyes on the DJ's setup, where a small meter glowed with a number. 94, it read. She did the halving in her head, stepping over a backpack. Eighty-five was eight hours. Eighty-eight was four. Ninety-one was two. Ninety-four was one. One hour, and the night was three hours long.

"Come on, closer," Noemie shouted, and Alexandra grabbed her wrist and pulled her sideways instead, toward the water table. "What?" Noemie yelled. Alexandra held up fingers, then pointed at her ears and then at the speakers. Noemie's face cleared. "Oh. Your ear thing." "One hour," Alexandra shouted back. "That meter says we get one hour right there."

They danced at the middle of the floor instead, where the bass still reached her ribs but her voice could be heard without screaming. Afterward, in the car, Paige twisted around from the front seat. "You looked radical out there, by the way. Like you planned it." Alexandra looked out the dark window at the gym lights sliding past. "I kind of did," she said, and Noemie laughed from the seat beside her, ears, for once, perfectly quiet.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: On a care label, an empty triangle means any bleach may be used, while a triangle with a cross through it means the garment must not be bleached.
story:
Carson stood in his grandma's laundry room holding his gym shirt at arm's length, which was as close as he wanted to get to it. After Saturday's game in the heat, the shirt could practically perspire on its own, and his grandma had declared that anyone old enough to sweat like that was old enough to do a wash. She had left him alone with the machine, a basket of clothes, and a jug of bleach, saying only, "Sort first, then read the labels," before going back to her Italian cuisine experiment in the kitchen, something that involved a whole head of garlic.

He sorted into piles on the tile floor: whites, darks, and a middle pile of things he couldn't decide about, including a red-striped shirt with a ketchup stain from lunch. The stain bugged him. His plan formed in a quick, spontaneous burst: whites and the striped shirt together, bleach in, stain gone, everything bright. He reached for the jug.

Then he remembered her words and flipped the striped shirt over, hunting for the label. Stitched inside the seam was a little triangle with a cross through it. He stared at it, then checked a white sock: its label showed a plain empty triangle with nothing inside. He held the two labels side by side. Same shape, different marks. If the empty one meant bleach was fine, then the crossed-out one had to mean the opposite, a do-not-enter sign for bleach. He thought of his cousin's shorts that had once come out of a wash blotchy and ruined, and how nobody would say why. Maybe this was why. He dropped the striped shirt into the middle pile and poured bleach only into the whites load.

When the machine was chugging, he texted Mario a photo of both labels: "laundry secret code." Mario replied with three mind-blown emojis.

His grandma came in later as he was folding the warm striped shirt, now washed with the darks, stain faded, stripes intact. She picked up the white sock, turned its label toward the light, and nodded slowly.

"Empty triangle," Carson said.

"Good," she said. "You'll do."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: When David Rudisha set the men's 800-metre world record at the 2012 London Olympics, his first lap was more than two seconds faster than his second.
story:
Blake crouched at the edge of the basketball court, tying his shoes for the third time, because Saturday morning drills had turned into time trials and he had one shot before the coach posted the roster. The court's sidelines doubled as a track loop around the gym, fourteen laps to a mile, and the eight-hundred was two of them. His problem was simple: every time he raced it, he exploded off the line, led the first lap, and then his legs deteriorated so badly that the last hundred metres felt like running through wet sand.

Imane jogged over, bouncing a basketball she had no intention of shooting. "Coach says you keep dying at the end," she said. "I told him it's not your legs, it's your plan." She wanted the roster spot too, but she had already run her trial, and now she seemed more interested in fixing him than beating him, which Blake decided not to question.

That night Blake watched the 2012 London Olympic final, David Rudisha's world record race, on his phone with Arwen, who kept pausing it to argue about which runner would fade. Blake made Arwen time each lap. When the numbers came up, he sat back on his bed. "Rudisha ran the first lap more than two seconds faster than his second," he said. Arwen frowned. "And he set the world record like that?" Blake nodded slowly, testing the idea out loud. "So the best eight-hundred runner ever didn't even split. He burned early and still had enough left."

The next Saturday he tried it on the court loop, with Imane calling lap times from the sideline. He went out hard, hard enough to frighten himself, then held a consistent rhythm instead of sprinting or sulking. Halfway through the second lap his legs burned, but they did not quit, because he hadn't wasted the first lap crawling. He crossed the line and bent over, gasping, while Imane squinted at her stopwatch and then showed him the time. It was three seconds faster than his last trial.

Mr. Rossi, who ran the gym on weekends, unlocked the water cooler and filled a cup without being asked. "You paced that," he said, handing it over.

Blake drank half and passed the cup to Imane, who had been shouting splits for twenty minutes in a dry throat. "Your turn to run," he said. "I'll call the numbers."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: On a river bend, water flows fastest on the outside, eroding that bank, and slowest on the inside, where it deposits sand and gravel.
story:
Jonathan stood where the creek bent just before it reached the beach, holding his sneakers in one hand and a red marker in the other. Tomorrow he had to explain to Ms. Doyle's class how a river carves a canyon over millions of years, and so far his practice speech had been six words long: "The water, um, goes through it." Harlee had laughed so hard at lunch that milk came out of her nose, which was not the review he was hoping for.

The creek gave him an idea. He waded in up to his ankles and dropped a handful of little paper boats upstream, boats he had folded from his notes that afternoon. Then he crouched at the bend and watched. The boats on the outside of the curve shot past him like they were fleeing the scene. The ones that drifted toward the inside of the bend slowed down, wobbled, and a few parked themselves on a low sandy shelf in the corner.

"Huh," Jonathan said out loud.

He looked at the two banks. On the outside of the bend, the bank was a steep, raw cut, dark soil hanging over the water in a ragged edge, with a pale scar above it where chunks had fallen away. On the inside, there was a small crescent of smooth sand mixed with gravel, dry and warm, like the creek had been building it out of leftovers. He picked up a pebble from that side and turned it over. Rounded. Well-traveled. Not the jagged stuff from the cut bank.

"You're going to get trench foot," said a voice behind him. Cynthia was coming down the beach path with an ice cream, which she pointed at him like evidence. "Also, why are there paper boats in the creek?"

"Experiment," Jonathan said. He explained the boats, the fast water, the slow water, the cut bank and the sandy side. "Outside of the bend, the water moves fastest, so it eats away that bank. Inside, it's slowest, so it drops the sand and gravel it's carrying."

Cynthia licked her ice cream and considered this. "So the creek is digging itself a valley? Like, over a long time?"

"Millions of years for a real canyon," Jonathan said, and as he said it he felt the speech assembling itself in his head, piece by piece, like the boats folding. "Bend by bend. Storm by storm."

"Ms. Doyle is going to weep with joy," Cynthia said. "Possibly literally. She cried when the class average went up two points."

He laughed, but then he stood there a minute longer, thinking about last month, when he'd blown off the first practice talk and gone to the arcade with Harlee instead. That had been a legitimate choice at the time, at least it had felt like one, and its consequence had been a D minus and his mother's face doing that complicated thing it did. He couldn't decide if the arcade had been worth it. The racing game had honestly been great. The D minus had honestly not been.

"I have to adjust my notes," he said suddenly. "All of them. The whole thing is wrong." His notes compared a canyon to a knife cutting a cake, which he now realized was exactly backwards. The river wasn't slicing. It was sweeping, carrying, dropping, one grain at a time, for longer than anyone could imagine.

He fished the boats out of the creek, wrung out his socks, and climbed the low dune to the dry sand where his backpack waited. He sat down, opened his notebook to a clean page, and wrote at the top, in big letters, THE BEND. Below it he drew two curving arrows, one fast, one slow.

"Say the fast arrow again," Cynthia said, sitting down beside him, "before I forget it for the quiz."

"Outside of the bend," Jonathan said, and started drawing the cut bank, steep and ragged, just like the real one behind him.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Teen safety guides advise telling a parent or trusted adult where you are going, who you will be with and when you will be home.
story:
Alexander stood at the kitchen counter with his phone in his hand and no words typed. In twenty minutes he was supposed to meet Tea at the bowling alley, his first actual date, and every part of him wanted to slip out the door like a ghost. Last summer, before Maxton moved away, they had ridden their bikes to the creek without telling anyone and come home to a search party of one frantic mother and two neighbours with flashlights. He remembered standing in the driveway, mud on his shoes, watching his mom's hands shake as she hugged him and then didn't let go for a long time.

That was the memory buzzing in his head now. He had started noticing a pattern since then: whenever he went somewhere without saying where, she texted him twice as often, sometimes three times in an hour. When he told her the plan, she barely texted at all. He wasn't sure it was a real rule or just coincidence, so last weekend he had tested it. Saturday he said nothing and went to Maxton's cousin's house; four texts arrived before noon. Sunday he announced, "Library, with Tea, home by four," and his phone stayed silent until she asked what he wanted for dinner. The evidence was pretty clear. Her worry wasn't random; it had a hidden cause, and the cause was the empty space where his plan should have been.

So tonight he started typing. He deleted it twice because it felt like something a little kid would do, then thought about Tea, who went to the prestigious math academy across town and once said her mom was "like a rudder, annoying and keeping us off the rocks." Then he typed it plainly: going to Pin City bowling with Tea, back by nine. He pressed send before he could change his mind.

His mom called from the living room. "Nine's fine. Do you have money for shoes?"

"Yeah. And fries."

"Take the umbrella anyway," she said, and he heard her turn the TV volume back up, which was the sound of her relaxing, though she would never disclose that in a million years.

At the door he almost bolted, but he stopped and called back, "It's a date, by the way. Like, a date date." A long pause came from the couch, then footsteps, and his mom appeared in the hallway holding the umbrella out to him with a grin he'd never seen before, half proud, half ready to cry.

"Strike on lane seven," she said. "That's all I'm saying."

activity: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
knowledge_domain: to compare a first-past-the-post election with proportional representation using a sample vote count
fact: Under proportional representation, parties win seats roughly in proportion to their share of the vote, so a party with 30 percent of the vote gets about 30 percent of the seats.
story:
Antoine pressed his nose against the gym door window and grinned. The polling station had real booths, a real box with a slot, and a volunteer who kept saying "Ballot here!" like a game show host. Mr. Ionescu had brought the whole class to watch democracy in action, and better yet, they each got a mock ballot to cast for a class council of five seats.

"Vote for one party," Milo read off his ballot. "Shark Party, Comet Party, or Sprout Party." Antoine marked Comet, Bently marked Shark, and they dropped their papers into the practice box the volunteer had set up for the class. Then Mr. Ionescu said the magic words: "You will count these yourselves, twice, with two different sets of rules. First count, the party with the most votes wins every seat. Ready?"

Antoine spread the forty ballots across the bleachers and counted like a squirrel counting acorns. Shark Party got twenty. Comet got twelve. Sprout got eight. Under the first-past-the-post rules, Shark swept all five seats, even though only half the class voted Shark. Bently did a touchdown dance. Milo groaned and threatened to intervene by eating the ballots, which was not actually a rule, but Mr. Ionescu let it slide since he only pretended.

"Now the second count," Mr. Ionescu said, handing them a chart. "This one is called proportional representation. The seats follow the votes." Antoine stared at the numbers. He grabbed his pencil and muttered, "If seats follow votes, then half the votes should mean half the seats." He tried it. Shark had half the vote, so Shark got about half the seats, two or three. Comet had twelve out of forty, which was thirty percent, so Comet should get about thirty percent of the seats. One and a half seats, which was obviously impossible, so he rounded and wrote two. Sprout's eight votes was twenty percent, so about one seat.

"Hold on," Milo said, leaning over his shoulder. "Comet gets two seats now? We got shut out before!" Antoine ran the check twice more, and the answer stayed consistent every time: under the proportional rules the council came out three Shark, two Comet, one Sprout, a completely different council from the same pile of ballots. "Same votes," Antoine said slowly, "different rules, different winners. The ballots didn't change. Only the counting did." He felt like a detective who had just found the real culprit, which was not Shark or Comet but the rule itself.

"Diagnosis," Bently announced, pointing at the first tally sheet. "The winner-take-all count has a case of the disappearing minorities." Milo laughed so hard he knocked a pencil off the bleachers. Antoine snapped a photo of both charts side by side and held it up. "Mr. Ionescu, can we present this to the class? Like, right now?" Mr. Ionescu checked his watch and nodded toward the gym doors. Antoine was already sprinting, charts flapping, shouting over his shoulder, "Last one to the classroom is a plurality!"

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In his 1872 book on emotions, Charles Darwin called blushing 'the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions'.
story:
Paige had spent forty minutes deciding between two shirts, and the winner was the one she was now sweating through. She waited by the mall fountain, watching the pennies glow at the bottom under the luminous blue lights, and telling herself that nobody had ever actually died of embarrassment. Probably. Her face felt like a stove burner turned up high, which was ridiculous, because Gage was just Gage, the same boy who had once eaten a crayon on a dare in third grade.

He showed up holding a pretzel the size of a steering wheel. "You bought food before the date started?" Paige asked.

"I was nervous, okay? Chewing helps." He offered her half, and she laughed, and then caught her reflection in the fountain glass. Her cheeks were the color of the ketchup packets on the pretzel stand's counter. "Great," she muttered. "I look like a stop sign."

"That's the blushing." Gage nodded like a professor. "Charles Darwin wrote about it. In his 1872 book on emotions, he called blushing 'the most peculiar and the most human of all expressions.'"

Paige stared at him. "You memorized that?"

"I read it last night. After I asked you out, my face went all red, so I looked it up. Darwin. Emotions. 1872. 'Most peculiar and most human of all expressions.' I wanted to, you know, know things."

She filed this away as the most adorable piece of homework anyone had ever done, but what she said was, "So it's human. Which means everyone does it. Which means I can figure out how to stop it." She was already planning the experiment. If she could eliminate the things that made her blush, one at a time, she could find the cause. Maybe it was eye contact. Maybe it was compliments. Maybe it was pretzels.

She tested her ideas at the arcade next door. Looking directly at Gage while he complimented her air hockey skills: red. Looking away while he said something silly: also red. Complimenting him instead: somehow worse, and he went red too, which made her go redder, which made him laugh, which made her laugh. Every variable she changed, the blush stayed. The pattern was obvious now. The only thing every case had in common was Gage himself.

"I can't eliminate you," she said, holding her air hockey paddle like evidence. "You're the cause."

"Wait," Gage said, going scarlet again. "That's the nicest thing anyone's ever proven to me."

Behind the counter, Mr. Moretti, the arcade owner, leaned over and squinted at them both. "You two are glowing like my jackpot machine. Somebody hit the jackpot?"

Paige looked at Gage. Gage looked at Paige. "Actually," she said, "I think we both did."

Mr. Moretti shrugged and slid two free tokens across the counter. "Most peculiar thing I've seen all day," he said, and rang the bell.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
The pimple had appeared on Tuesday, right on the tip of Maelie's chin, and by Friday it had invited two friends. She stood in the face wash aisle of Hartley's Pharmacy, holding her phone against her cheek so Dania could see the wall of bottles through the video call.

"There are like forty kinds," Maelie said. "Salicylic acid, benzoyl peroxide, foaming, non-foaming, sensitive skin, oily skin. How am I supposed to know which one?"

"Pick the cheapest one with a shark on it," Dania said. "Sharks are cool."

"There is no shark one." Maelie turned the phone to prove it.

Finn leaned into the frame from beside Dania, holding a bag of chips. "My brother just uses soap. Regular soap. His face looks fine."

Maelie thought about that. Finn's brother was fourteen and had a face like a clean plate, which was honestly annoying. But her own face had been fine too, all last year. Something had changed between then and now, and regular soap had not changed with it. She turned a bottle over and read the back label, hunting for a clue.

The label said "controls excess oil," and that word snagged in her mind. Excess. That meant more than normal, more than before. She picked up another bottle. Also oil control. A third one, aimed at teenagers, said it "removes oil that clogs pores." Clogs. Pores. She remembered the health unit in September, Ms. Kelly passing around a diagram of skin layers, and one sentence she had half-listened to came back with sudden, acute clarity: hormones in puberty make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil. More oil, and the oil had a name.

"Sebum," Maelie said out loud.

"What?" said Dania.

"Sebum. That's the oil. It's called sebum." She said it again, testing it. "Hormones in puberty make your oil glands make more of it, and it clogs your pores, and that's the pimples. That's why it's happening now and not in fourth grade."

"So your face is a hormone crime scene," Finn said.

"Basically." Maelie lined up three bottles on the shelf edge and read the fine print on each one. This was like a lab, she decided. The hidden cause was the extra sebum, so the face wash should target oil. The one for "sensitive skin" said nothing about oil. Out. The foaming one with benzoyl peroxide said it unclogged pores, and the salicylic acid one said it cleared away oil. Both attacked the actual cause. She chose the salicylic one because it was a dollar less, and because the benzoyl peroxide bottle warned it could bleach towels, and she owned exactly one good towel.

At the register, Ms. Kelly from down the street was buying bandages for her dog, and she smiled at the bottle in Maelie's hand. "Good choice. Took me a whole summer to figure that out at your age."

Maelie paid, pocketed the change, and walked home with the bottle in her backpack like evidence. That night she washed her face, and the next morning, and the morning after that. By Sunday the original pimple had gone quiet, and though the two friends were still there, they were smaller, retreating. She took a photo of her chin, then another on Wednesday, and laid them side by side to distinguish the before from the after. The difference was small but real, and she had found it herself, one label at a time.

"Your face looks better," her mom said at breakfast.

"Inference from evidence," Maelie said, pointing at the photos. Then she went to the bathroom mirror, tilted her chin up, and grinned at it.

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: To finish 800 metres in three minutes on a 400-metre track, a runner must average 90 seconds for each lap.
story:
Paisley pinned her race number to her shirt, then flipped it over and wrote on the back with a stub of pencil. Ms. Tesfaye had said the tryout standard for the relay squad was three minutes for eight hundred metres, two laps of the park track. Paisley chewed the pencil. Three minutes was one hundred and eighty seconds, and one hundred and eighty split across two laps was ninety each. She wrote "90" twice and circled it.

"Are you doing math at a track?" Francesca asked, leaning over her shoulder. "That's like doing cartwheels in a library."

"It's my lap target," Paisley said. "If I want three minutes for eight hundred metres on this four-hundred-metre track, I have to average ninety seconds a lap. Both laps. Not a fast one and a disaster one."

"You always do the fast one and the disaster one," Eleni said from the bench, lacing her spikes. "Last week you went out like a rocket and then jogged the second lap like you were touring a garden."

"That was strategy," Paisley said.

"That was you lying on the grass making whale sounds," Francesca said.

The whistle blew. Paisley tucked the number into her waistband, took the inside lane, and told herself the number: ninety, ninety. Francesca waved a clipboard from the fence. The gun cracked and Paisley went out hard anyway, because her legs had opinions of their own, and she hit the first lap feeling wonderful and winded.

Then she saw Francesca's face. Francesca was holding up the clipboard with a number on it, and it was not 90. Paisley's stomach dropped as she started the second lap with her lungs burning. She made a quick pivot at the bend to avoid a walker who had wandered onto lane one, and the stumble cost her a beat. Her legs filled with sand. She crossed the line and bent over, hands on knees, sure she had ruined it.

"Two fifty-eight," Francesca announced, showing the stopwatch like a prize fish.

"Wait, what was the first lap?" Paisley gasped.

"Eighty-four. You went out six seconds too fast, you absolute rocket, and then you dragged yourself home in eighty-four... no, seventy-four." Francesca tapped her watch. "The math saved you anyway. You had enough to squeak under."

Eleni jogged over. "I was pessimistic about your second lap. I apologize. I accuse your legs of knowing more than your head."

"I changed my mind about the whole thing," Paisley said, still breathing hard, but grinning now. "Even splits are boring and they work."

Ms. Tesfaye wrote something on her list, then looked up. "Paisley. Relay squad. Monday, four o'clock."

Paisley unpinned her number, held up the back with the two circled nineties, and showed it to Francesca. "Ninety and ninety," she said. "Same time, twice."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Stress can show up in the body as headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms or trouble falling asleep.
story:
The waiting room had four chairs, a sparse rack of pamphlets, and a fish tank with one tired fish circling it. Ryan sat with his hands pressed flat on his knees so nobody would notice they were damp again. His head had hurt since Tuesday, and his stomach felt tight every morning, and last night he had lain awake until almost one. His mom had finally made the appointment.

Mr. Morales came out in a white coat and read the chart. "Headaches three days, stomach bothering you, trouble sleeping." He looked up. "Any fever? Anything you ate?"

"No fever. It's like my stomach clenches, and then it lets go, and then it clenches." Ryan wiped his palms on his jeans. "They sweat. Even now, in air conditioning."

Mr. Morales tapped his pen twice against the clipboard, then asked the question nobody had asked yet. "Is anything big coming up? Something you've been thinking about a lot?"

Ryan opened his mouth to say no, because that would have been the simple answer, and the whole room seemed to slow down. He thought about Sunday night, lying awake. About Monday morning, stomach tight in the car. About the same thing the Monday before. The pattern lined up in his head like a sequence he'd never bothered to run. "There's a track tryout," he said. "Friday. I keep going over it. Even when I don't want to."

"There it is," said Mr. Morales quietly. "Stress can show up in the body exactly like this. Headaches, a tight or upset stomach, sweaty palms, trouble falling asleep. Your body's been telling you what your head wouldn't say out loud."

They tried something right there. Mr. Morales had Ryan breathe in for four counts, hold, let it out slow, like he was fogging a window. Twice. Three times. The tightness in his stomach eased a fraction, enough that Ryan noticed its absence, which was strange and good. That night, instead of lying in the dark going over the tryout, he installed a routine: phone charging across the room, window cracked, lights out at ten, the slow breathing until his thoughts went soft. He slept through until morning.

At school on Thursday, Talia caught him counting under his breath outside the gym. "Are you okay?"

"Practicing," he said, and let the breath out slow, like fog on glass. "Friday we find out if it works."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In one-point perspective, all lines going straight back into the distance meet at a single vanishing point on the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.
story:
Lea pressed her pencil so hard against the sketchpad that the street she was drawing looked like it had crashed. The left edge of the road slanted one way, the right edge slanted another, and the sidewalk lines wandered off toward the ceiling of the community art studio like they had somewhere better to be. Across the table, Brayden leaned over his own drawing of a taco truck and grinned.

"Your street is haunted," he said. "Mine's just hungry."

"Mine's supposed to be the road to summer camp," Lea said. "From the postcard my cousin sent." She held up the postcard, which showed a neat road shrinking toward the lake, and frowned at her paper. Somewhere between the real road and her page, three different sets of lines had decided to go three different directions. Scarlett, working at the easel beside them, peeked over and winced theatrically, which was not helpful.

Lea flipped the postcard over and found a message in her cousin's looping handwriting: "Dear Lea, camp is great. The cook makes a whole new cuisine every night, last week was noodles shaped like canoes. P.S. Mr. Foster says roads don't get wider as they go, they get narrower, and everything that goes straight back runs to one dot. Ask him what it's called. Also send snacks." Lea read it twice. One dot. She grabbed a fresh sheet and drew a flat line across the middle, then picked a point on it. She ran the road edges toward that single point, then the sidewalk lines, then the door lines, all of them, like strings on a kite converging at one place. The street snapped into depth so suddenly she laughed out loud.

"Vanishing point," said Mr. Foster from the doorway, holding two mugs of cocoa. "That's what it's called. And that line is the horizon, right at your eye level." He set a mug beside her elbow. "You found it on your own, so you get the good cocoa." Lea slid the second sheet over to Brayden, who had given his taco truck four vanishing points and one very dormant-looking customer asleep against the wheel.

"Fix it," she said. "One dot. That's the rule."

"Fine," Brayden said, "but if my truck still looks haunted, I'm blaming your cousin." He erased, drew a single point on his horizon line, and started over, tongue poking out the corner of his mouth.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Hostile attribution bias is the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident.
story:
The basketball court at Riverside Park was damp from the morning sprinklers, and Joseph noticed it first because his sneakers slid a little when he pivoted for a layup. He and Harper had been meeting here every Saturday since fifth grade, and today Harper was late, which was unusual, because Harper was never late for basketball.

When Harper finally arrived, he didn't say much. He just asked for the ball, drove toward the hoop, and called almost nothing. Joseph threw him a pass along the baseline and Harper's foot shot out from under him on the wet patch. The ball bounced away and rolled to the fence.

"Nice pass," Harper said, flat.

"You slipped," Joseph said. "It's wet right there."

"Sure it is."

Joseph picked up the ball and stood still for a second, thinking. Yesterday at lunch, a kid had jostled Joseph's tray in the cafeteria line, and Joseph had spent the whole afternoon convinced it was deliberate. Then the kid had pointed at the puddle of milk on the floor, and Joseph had felt his certainty drain away. Mr. Clarke, who ran the after-school science club, had a poster about that kind of thinking. It was called hostile attribution bias, the tendency to assume someone meant to hurt you when what they did was unclear or could easily have been an accident. Joseph had read it twice and thought it was naive to imagine people were always innocent, but the poster stuck with him anyway.

He wondered whether the same thing was happening now, in reverse. Harper thought the pass was aimed at his feet, but Joseph knew it wasn't. What he couldn't see was why Harper believed it. Maybe something else had happened, something Joseph hadn't noticed. He decided to test it, the way they tested ideas in science club. He walked over to the wet spot and stood on it.

"Come here," he said. "Stand on this."

"Why?"

"Just do it."

Harper came over, stepped where Joseph pointed, and slid half an inch. He looked down at the shine on the concrete, then back at the fence, then at the ground again. "Oh," he said.

"That's what happened," Joseph said. "I didn't aim it there. I didn't even know it was slippery until you went down."

Harper dribbled the ball once, slowly. "Heidi told me you said my jump shot was ugly," he said. "At lunch on Thursday."

Joseph blinked. "I said it was weird. I meant the way you kick your leg out. Heidi always makes things sound worse than they are, you know that." He thought about telling Harper that assuming the worst had made everything look like an attack, the way Joseph had assumed the worst about the tray. Instead he just said, "You want me to say it's ugly? Fine, it's ugly. It's also the best shot in the park."

Harper laughed, a real one this time, and checked up for the ball.

They played until the sun dropped behind the rec center. Near the end, Harper took a shot from the corner, leg kicking out like always, and it rattled in. He pointed at the wet patch on his way back down the court. "Still slippery," he said. "Watch your feet."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: Portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage.
story:
The lights went out at half past six, and Sophie's whole street went dark with them. Her mother found a flashlight and said the outage could last all night, so Sophie walked two houses down to check on Mr. Demetriou, the widower at the end of the block who lived alone in the biggest residence on the street. She could see a flashlight swinging in his garage, its beam cutting across the driveway, so she crossed the frosty grass and knocked on the side door.

"Come in, come in," he called. Inside, the garage smelled of gasoline and old paint. A portable generator sat in the middle of the floor, and Mr. Demetriou was feeding it a fresh can of fuel. "This old thing will run my refrigerator and a lamp or two," he said, wiping his hands on a rag. "Been sitting in here since the last storm."

Sophie's stomach tightened. Last term, her science teacher had handed out a safety sheet they'd all had to read aloud, and one line had stuck with her because she'd gotten it wrong on the quiz: portable generators and charcoal grills give off carbon monoxide, so safety agencies say to run them only outdoors, far from doors and windows, never in a house or garage. She had marked "garage with the door open" as safe. It was not.

"Wait," she said. "You can't start it in here. It gives off carbon monoxide. It has to be outside, far away from doors and windows. Never in a house or a garage. Not even the garage."

Mr. Demetriou frowned at the machine as if it had betrayed him. "My neighbour ran his in the garage for years."

"That's what the safety agencies say anyway," Sophie said. "We had to memorize it." She remembered how tedious that worksheet had been, thirty identical questions about invisible gas, and how she'd complained to Eva that none of it would ever matter. She texted Eva now, in the dark of the garage: you will not believe this.

They wrestled the generator out together, its wheels squealing across the concrete, and positioned it at the far end of the backyard where the grass gave way to woods. The extension cords had to be daisy-chained through a window Mr. Demetriou cracked open just wide enough for the plugs, and the refrigerator ended up too far from the kitchen to matter. The lamp worked, though, and he insisted Sophie take a peanut butter cookie for her trouble.

By the time she got home, her own house had decided to go to bed early, candles guttering on the kitchen table, her mother already asleep on the couch with the cat colonizing the warm spot beside her. Sophie stood at the window and looked down the street. Mr. Demetriou's backyard glowed with one small lamp out in the cold, and one dim window above it, and nothing else for blocks in any direction. She texted Eva again: told you. Told you what? came the reply. Sophie watched the little light flicker at the edge of the woods and typed, never mind, and put her phone face down on the sill.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: The word algebra comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.
story:
Ariana slid her worksheet across the table so Rylen could see it. "I keep getting x equals negative two, but the answer key says three." Math club met on Thursdays in Ms. MacLeod's room, and today the whole table smelled like the orange peels Asiya kept in her pencil case.

Ms. MacLeod leaned over the paper. "Show me what you did to both sides." Ariana pointed at her work. She had subtracted four from the left side of the equation but forgotten the right side entirely. "There's your ghost," Ms. MacLeod said. "You moved a number without paying it back."

"It's like a trade," Asiya said, pulling the orange peel out with her teeth and talking around it anyway. "Whatever you do on the left, you have to do on the right, or the whole thing tips over." Ariana tried the problem again, subtracting four from both sides this time, then dividing both sides by three. Three. It worked, and something in her chest loosened.

After the practice problems, Ms. MacLeod announced the club's next project: each member had to research one word from mathematics and present it. Ariana wanted something no one else would pick. At home that night she opened her laptop and searched the word algebra, mostly because it was the word that had been ruining her Tuesdays since September. She read the first result twice, then a second website to be sure.

The next morning she found Rylen at his locker. "You know where algebra got its name? It comes from al-jabr, part of the title of a book written around 820 CE in Baghdad by the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi." Rylen blinked. "Wait, algebra is a person's book?" "Part of a book title, in Arabic," Ariana said. "It's like if we called the whole subject one chapter heading." She had written the words in her notebook, al-jabr, and copied the name al-Khwarizmi twice so she would not mangle it in front of everyone.

At the following meeting she tested her idea for the presentation on Asiya and Rylen first, because presenting to friends was like distributing the scary part of a speech across more shoulders, so each person carried only a little. She drew a balance scale on the board, an unknown x on one pan, numbers on the other. "Al-Khwarizmi was balancing things over a thousand years before this worksheet," she said, holding it up. Asiya raised her hand as if they were in class. "So when I subtract four from only one side, I'm breaking a rule that old?" Ariana nodded, then paused, marker hovering. Ms. MacLeod was writing something on a network of whiteboards she had connected across the back wall, and Ariana wondered whether al-Khwarizmi had ever suspected his book's title would end up printed on endangered worksheets in a folder that had survived three years of middle school. She capped the marker and turned back to her friends. "Okay, ask me the hard questions now."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The Stanley Cup was donated by Lord Stanley, Canada's governor general, in 1892 and first awarded in 1893, making it the oldest trophy in North American professional sports.
story:
The community rink had pulled a big screen down over the boards for the playoff game, and half the town sat in the cold bleachers with blankets and hot chocolate. Noah came with his dad and his sister, and he saved seats for Amar and Quincy, who arrived just before the puck dropped, cheeks red from the walk. Between periods, the zamboni droned around the ice while a man in a rink jacket carried out a replica of the Stanley Cup and set it on a table by the snack bar, where kids lined up to have their photos taken with it.

"It looks terrible," Quincy said, squinting at the replica's dented bowl and scratched bands. "Couldn't they polish it or something?"

"That's the real one on TV sometimes," Amar said. "It's all beat up there too. It's supposed to look brand new, isn't it?"

Noah looked at the dents and thought about it. New trophies look shiny because they are new, so an old-looking trophy might just be an old trophy. If the Cup had been around longer than any other trophy in North American professional sports, the dents made sense: more years of hands, more parades, more dropped on more locker room floors. He turned the idea over while the second period started behind them, and then he borrowed Amar's phone, typed a few words, and read down the page.

"I figured it out," Noah said, holding the phone out. "It looks old because it is old. Lord Stanley donated it, back in 1892. He was Canada's governor general. They first gave it out in 1893. It's the oldest trophy in North American professional sports."

Quincy did the math on his fingers. "That's over a hundred years of getting banged up."

"Exactly," Noah said.

The man in the rink jacket came back to move the table, because the recession had cut the rink's budget and the cup replica was rented by the hour now. He listened for a second and nodded. "You've done your homework," he said, and let Noah's sister touch the base, though not the bowl.

Behind them the crowd made a noise like a wave, and the third period was starting. The window beside the screen had gone opaque with frost, and Noah wiped a circle in it with his sleeve so they could see the real ice below, empty and white under the lights. Amar pointed at the score on the big screen. "Two minutes left and we're up by one."

Noah grabbed the edge of the bleacher. "Come on," he said. "Kill the clock."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Día de los Muertos, celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas.
story:
Eli's mother had set up the altar on the coffee table before he got home from school, and now the whole living room smelled of marigolds and pan dulce. November had arrived, and with it the boxes from the hall closet: the folded purple paper, the candles, the little clay skeleton playing a guitar. His grandmother had taught his mother how to build it years ago, and his mother had kept the tradition going ever since they moved.

"Día de los Muertos," his mother said to Arnav and Jazmin, who had come over with their boxes of craft supplies, "celebrated in Mexico mainly on November 1 and 2, honors family members who have died with home altars called ofrendas."

"Ofrendas," Jazmin repeated, sounding it out carefully.

Arnav crouched and studied the tiers. Candles on top, fruit on the second level, a small bowl of salt. He pointed at a framed photograph of an old man in a barber's apron. "Who's that?"

"My abuelo Ramón," Eli said. "He cut hair in the same shop for forty years. The chairs he bought in 1962 were still durable when he retired. Customers sat in them until the day he closed the doors."

Jazmin pulled a photo from her backpack, one she'd brought from home, and set it beside Ramón's: a man in a military uniform, her bisabuelo. "My great-grandfather," she said. "I've never done this before. My family doesn't really do holidays."

Eli wanted to say something welcoming, but something about the altar was bothering him, and he couldn't stop staring at it. His mother always laid a path of marigold petals from the front door to the table, so the dead could follow it home. This year there was no path, and there was no jar of the cinnamon candy Ramón had kept in a dish by his mirror for as long as Eli could remember. Eli had eaten one at every haircut, age four through age eleven.

He went to the kitchen where his mother was heating champurrado. "The altar's missing the candy," he said. "And the petals."

She didn't turn around. "I know. I couldn't find the dish."

"Then how does he find his way?" Eli asked. "How does he know it's for him?"

His mother finally looked at him, and something tired crossed her face. "Maybe I thought it didn't matter this year. It's a lot of work to sustain all by myself."

Eli stood there holding that. Last year he had been at Arnav's house playing video games while his mother laid out the petals alone. He remembered glancing at the time, thinking he should go home, and not going.

"Arnav," he called into the living room, "does your mom still have those marigolds on the porch?" Then he was out the front door, counting the orange blooms in the neighbor's window box, and Arnav came back with a fistful of stems, and Jazmin tore sheets of orange paper into petals when the real flowers ran short. They laid the trail from the doorstep, over the carpet, up to the coffee table. Eli dug through the pantry until he found a bag of cinnamon candies left over from Halloween and poured them into a juice glass.

"There," he said, placing the glass next to Ramón's photograph, where the dish used to sit.

His mother came in with four mugs of champurrado and stopped in the doorway. She looked at the petal path, then at the glass, then at the three of them sitting on the floor around the altar.

"Forty years of haircuts," Jazmin said, raising her mug toward the photograph, "and he never ran out of candy."

"He never ran out of stories either," Eli's mother said, and she sat down on the floor with them.

Eli took one cinnamon candy from the glass and let it burn sweet on his tongue.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Historians check a diary against other sources, such as letters, newspapers and government records, to test whether its details are accurate.
story:
Joseph had exactly one hour before the archive closed, and one diary page to figure out. The diary belonged to a settler named Amos Pike, and Mr. Gupta had laid it on a foam wedge with a page weight so frail it looked like a butterfly pinned in place. Joseph's project question was simple: why did people move west in the 1800s? Amos's entry said his family left Ohio because the river flood ruined their corn and their money was gone. That was an answer. It just wasn't a proven one yet.

Karlee leaned over his shoulder, tapping the photocopied page with one finger. "It's perfect. It says right there, April 14, 1847, flood took the fields. Put it on the poster and we're done." She wanted the poster done, wanted the blue ribbon at the history fair, and mostly wanted to stop squinting at old handwriting. Joseph didn't answer right away. Something about the date was bothering him, the way a frayed tendon bothers a runner: you can keep going, but you feel it every step.

He pulled the microfilm reel of the county newspaper that Mr. Gupta had left on the cart, the same spring, 1847. Karlee groaned but helped him crank the handle, page after page swimming past. April. May. Then Joseph stopped cranking. The paper's whole front page was about the flood. The date on the masthead was April 2, 1847. Twelve days before Amos claimed it happened. "Which one's wrong?" Karlee whispered, as if the dead printer might hear.

Joseph thought about it out loud, because thinking alone wasn't getting him anywhere. "If the newspaper is wrong, then the whole county printed the wrong date. If the diary is wrong, then one tired man writing by candlelight made a mistake. But maybe the diary isn't wrong. Maybe he wrote about it twelve days later, like catching up." They checked the letters folder Mr. Gupta had pulled, a government relief record listing families who lost crops. Amos Pike's name was there, and the flood was there, and when Joseph set the diary beside the letters, the newspaper, and the record, every one of them told the same story with slightly different dates. He sat back. "That's what historians do. They check a diary against other sources, letters, newspapers, government records, to test whether its details are accurate."

Mr. Gupta drifted over and read their three documents spread side by side. He raised an eyebrow at Joseph, who felt something propel him out of his chair to grab a pencil. "We can show the flood in the newspaper, the diary saying why they left, and the relief record proving it," Joseph said. "Not just one source. Three." Karlee was already sketching a headline across the poster board: THE FLOOD THAT PUSHED THEM WEST. "Fine," she said, "but I get to draw the river." She uncapped a blue marker, and the water rose across the page.

activity: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
knowledge_domain: to write a thesis statement and outline a three-point argument before drafting
fact: An outline lists the main points and their evidence before drafting, so a writer can spot a weak or missing point before spending time on full paragraphs.
story:
Mr. Rowe's cafe had one rule written on the chalkboard: buy something, stay as long as you like. Michael bought the smallest hot chocolate available and spread his essay prompt across the window table. The essay was due Monday, and today was Saturday, and the prompt asked him to argue whether the school should add a later start time. He had a thesis, or something like one, scribbled on his hand: "Later start times are good." He suspected it was not good.

Timothy slid into the chair across from him with a muffin he had clearly bought only to comply with the chalkboard. "What's that on your hand?"

"My thesis statement," Michael said, and watched Timothy's face do the polite thing.

"It's a whole sentence?"

"It's a whole opinion." Michael turned his hand over. There was a smear of chocolate on the other side, so now he had a thesis and a stain, roughly equal in persuasive power.

Rylan arrived, took one look at the prompt, and pulled a napkin from the dispenser. "My sister failed this class. She says you make an outline first. It lists your main points and the evidence for each one, before you write anything." She drew three boxes. "You put a point in each box, and the evidence under it."

"That's a lot of boxes for a napkin," Timothy said.

Michael took the pen anyway. Point one: teenagers need more sleep. Evidence: his own life, plus a study Mr. Rowe's nephew had once mentioned at the counter. Point two: attendance would improve. Evidence: Rylan said her sister's school tried it, and fewer people skipped first period. Point three: grades would go up. He sat with the pen above the third box for a long moment.

"Nothing?" Rylan said.

"Nothing." He had believed grades would go up with his whole heart about ninety seconds ago. Now that he had to name the evidence, the belief seemed to evaporate. "It's probably true, but I can't prove it's probable, if that makes sense."

"It doesn't," Timothy said, but he was reading the napkin.

Michael looked at the napkin, then at the smear on his hand, then at the napkin again. The outline had caught the weak point in under five minutes. If he'd written three full paragraphs, the third one would have been two hundred words of confident nothing, and he would have found that out from a grade on Thursday. The napkin was faster and cheaper, and it had cost him one napkin.

He crossed out the third box and wrote a new one: later start times help student athletes, because practice schedules shift too. Evidence: Timothy, who played soccer, said morning practices were a mechanism for producing zombies. Timothy objected to being cited, then objected again when Michael wrote "personal interview" under his name.

Mr. Rowe came over with a rag and a refill nobody ordered. He glanced at the napkin, said nothing, and cleared the muffin wrapper. At the counter he did write something, though, small, near the register: Saturday regulars, one free cocoa.

Michael folded the napkin into his pocket. "Three points, all with evidence."

"Two points and me," Timothy said.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The parable of the blind men and the elephant, from ancient India, describes people who each touch a different part of an elephant and describe it completely differently.
story:
Naomi arrived at the science club room holding one end of a rolled-up poster, and Cohen held the other, and they were already arguing before they got through the door.

"It's a river mouth," Cohen said. "That's what we're presenting. The estuary, where the river meets the sea."

"It's a wetland," said Lillian from the back table, where she was taping a board she had painted green. "Birds, reeds, mudflats. That's the whole project."

They had been building the model for three weeks, but each of them had only worked on a Wednesday, and only on their own section, because Ms. Carvalho had said the club was too big for everyone to crowd around one table. Naomi had the waves. Cohen had the river. Lillian had the marsh. None of them had seen the others' parts until today, when they tried to fit the pieces together and the river ran uphill into the birds.

Naomi sat down and pulled out her notebook. On Monday, in English, the teacher had read them a story from ancient India, a parable about blind men and an elephant. Each man touched a different part, and the one who felt the trunk said the elephant was like a snake, and the one who felt the leg said it was like a tree, and they described it completely differently because each had only touched one piece.

"We're the blind men," Naomi said. "The elephant. Look it up."

Cohen did, on the club laptop, and read silently, and his face changed. "Okay," he said quietly. "Okay, that's us."

"So what do we do?" Lillian asked. She was still holding her tape, and Naomi could tell she didn't want her marsh moved, because Lillian had stayed late twice to paint the birds' legs, and nobody had said anything about it.

"Friday, we all come on the same day," Naomi said. "And we integrate the sections before we build more. All three of us. Nobody works alone."

Lillian wrote something on a scrap of paper and slid it across the table instead of answering out loud, which was what she did when she was deciding. Naomi unfolded it. "My marsh goes last, then, right? Because the estuary part is the best part. Don't shove my birds in a corner." Naomi wrote back, "Front and center, I promise," and Lillian read it and gave one short nod, and Naomi felt buoyant, almost floating, because it had worked.

It worked, and it cost them. Nobody's piece stayed exactly as it had been. Cohen's river had to bend twice, and Naomi's waves had to shrink, and on Friday they stayed until the janitor jingled his keys at the door. But when they carried the model to the front table, the water ran downhill, all the way from the river through the marsh to the sea.

"There," said Cohen.

"Almost perfect," said Lillian, touching one small painted wing with her fingertip.

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: The hottest weeks usually come several weeks after the summer solstice, because land and oceans take time to warm up.
story:
Ariana had one more chance to pass Ms. Chukwu's seasons retake on Monday, and she was determined to crack it before then, even if that meant hauling a flashlight, a grapefruit, and a skewer to the beach on a Saturday. Farrah spread the towel while Sofie dug through the cooler like a scavenger hunting for the last juice box. "You're going to teach a grapefruit about Earth," Sofie said. "I'm going to teach you," Ariana said, "and then you're going to quiz me until I can't get it wrong."

She pushed the skewer through the grapefruit at a slant and held it up. "Okay. Earth's axis isn't straight up and down. It's tilted, and it stays tilted the same way while Earth goes around the sun." She swept the fruit in a slow circle, flashlight beaming from a beach chair. "When our half is tilted toward the sun, the light hits us more directly and the days are longer. That's summer." Farrah leaned in, squinting. "So it's not because we're closer to the sun?" "That's what I said on the test," Ariana admitted. "That's what got me the retake."

Sofie took over the flashlight and circled it the wrong way twice before Farrah enforced the correct direction, turning Ariana's shoulders like a turntable until she groaned and laughed. The warm sand shifted under their knees. A gull stalked the cooler, sideways and shameless, and Sofie guarded the sandwiches like it was a paid job.

Then Farrah frowned. "Wait. So the longest day of the whole year is the first day of summer, right? The solstice. Wouldn't that also be the hottest day?" Ariana opened her mouth to say obviously, and then stopped, because she remembered the calendar from the retake review sheet, the one she'd photographed on her phone. She scrolled and held it out. "Look. The longest day was weeks ago, and the forecast this week is still the hottest of the summer." She turned the grapefruit slowly, thinking. "So the tilt gives you the longest day, but the heat takes longer to arrive." Sofie picked up a handful of sand. "Like this. The sun's been beating on it all day, and it's still cool underneath." "The land and oceans take time to warm up," Ariana said. "The heat builds gradually. It lags behind."

They sat with that for a minute, the waves ticking in and out. Farrah picked up the flashlight. "Okay, final quiz. Explain summer and winter to the seagull." The gull stared at them with one orange eye, entirely unimpressed. Ariana held up the grapefruit, cleared her throat, and began, "Sir, imagine you are a large citrus planet."

Sofie fell over sideways into the sand, laughing. Farrah raised the flashlight solemnly, like a judge at a citrus science fair, and said, "One more time, from the top."

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
The note on the fridge had said "your turn," so Savannah dragged the laundry bag two blocks to the Spin Cycle Laundromat, where Louis-Thomas was already waiting with his own basket and a bag of chips. She dumped everything on the folding table and started making piles. Whites, darks, and a suspicious middle pile that contained her dad's pink-ish sock, a shirt with a bee on it from their science unit about how insects pollinate flowers, and Channing's spare shirt from the class hamster's cage, which smelled like rodent even from a distance. She sniffed it, gagged, and threw it in with the darks. Probably fine.

While the washing machine churned, Mr. Kamau, who ran the place, set a battered iron on the counter beside the board. "The dance costume shirt your mother dropped off needs pressing before your recital," he said. "Delicate nylon. Do you know your iron symbols?" Savannah did not, but she said she'd figure it out, because the shirt had a tag with a little iron outline and one single dot inside it.

She turned the iron's dial while Louis-Thomas leaned in to watch. The dial had names, not dots. Nylon, silk, wool, cotton, linen. Which one meant one dot? She thought about the shirts in her closet, how the thick cotton ones could take heat and the slippery nylon ones felt like they might melt into pudding. Maybe the dots were a kind of ladder. "One dot's got to be low," she said slowly. "Two dots would be medium, three high. Like, three dots is around two hundred degrees, two is about one fifty, and one dot's the coolest, around one hundred ten." Louis-Thomas looked skeptical. "You just made that up." "I'm testing it," Savannah said, and set the dial to the lowest setting.

She waited for the iron to warm, then touched it to a hidden corner of the shirt. The fabric stayed dull and smooth. She pressed the front panel, and the wrinkles fell out like they were embarrassed to be there. Louis-Thomas grabbed a science worksheet from his backpack and held it up. "One dot means low. It's like the shirt is telling you its limit."

Channing arrived just in time to see the finished shirt gleaming on a hanger. "Whoa. Last time my mom ironed that thing on cotton, the whole front went shiny, like it was made of tinfoil." Savannah smiled and held up the tag, pointing at the dot.
