The washing machine buzzed behind her, and she was already pulling the warm load out, snapping a towel flat to fold it, one dot's worth of caution in her hands.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, starting the California Gold Rush that drew people west in huge numbers.
story:
Muhammad found the diary in a trunk at his grandfather's house, wedged between a quilt and a tin of buttons. It had a cracked leather cover and an entry dated March 1849. He had a history project due Monday: use a primary source to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. He had planned to look up old newspapers at the library, but here was the real thing, written by a man named Josiah who had actually gone.

He sat at the kitchen table and photographed the pages with his phone so he could read them at home. His grandfather set down a plate of bread and peanut butter. "That's nutritious enough to keep you going while you read," he said, and went back to weeding the garden.

The first entries were what Muhammad expected. Josiah wrote about poor soil back in Ohio, about land costing too much, about wanting a farm of his own out west where a man could claim acreage. Muhammad nodded along. That fit the textbook chapter about cheap land pulling settlers onto the Oregon Trail. Then he turned the page and stopped.

Josiah's handwriting got sloppier. "Brother Nathan has the fever," the entry read. "Talks of nothing but California. Says a man scooped gold out of a millrace with his bare hands. I told him a farm is a sure thing and gold is not, but he packed the wagon anyway." Muhammad read the line twice. Gold. He had assumed everyone in the diary was traveling for farmland, but Nathan was going for money. His first explanation covered only half the story.

He texted Daxton, who was doing the same project. Daxton wrote back that his source was a letter from a woman heading to Oregon, all about land. Muhammad typed: mine has a guy chasing gold. He checked the date in the diary, January 1848 in the margin of one entry, and looked it up on his phone. Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill in California in January 1848, and that started the California Gold Rush. So Nathan's "fever" had a real start date, and thousands of others had caught it too.

But Muhammad wanted to be sure his reading of the diary was right and not just a guess. He tested it by reading every 1849 entry in order. Nathan's letters home, quoted in the diary, mentioned San Francisco prices and mining camps, never crops. The farm talk came only from Josiah. Two brothers, two different reasons, in the same trunk. Muhammad decided to structure his project around that contrast instead of one single cause, and let the diary's own words serve as the evidence. When his grandfather came in from the garden, Muhammad held up the phone with the photographed pages. "This diary just settled my verdict on the whole project," he said. "Land and gold. Both pulled people west."

His grandfather dried his hands and leaned over the table. "Read me the part about the fever," he said.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Cutting an onion in half from top to root and laying each half flat side down gives a steady base, so the onion cannot roll while you slice it.
story:
The onion rolled off the table for the third time, and Nora caught it against her chest like a runaway hamster. "Okay," she said, holding it up to the gray morning sky. "You win this round."

The camp table wobbled on one short leg, and every time she set the onion down and reached for the knife, the whole table tilted and the onion took off. Kelly-Anne watched from the picnic bench, munching a dry cracker. "Maybe the onion doesn't want to be sauce," she said. "Maybe it's pessimistic about its future."

"Everything here is going in the sauce," Nora said. "Onions, tomatoes, garlic. Mr. Foster says if we make the sauce from scratch, we get first pick of the pasta tonight. The other cabin gets the jar stuff."

Ayla came over from the fire, wiping her hands on her shorts. "Coach says the pot's hot in ten minutes. How's the famous onion coming?" She picked it up, turned it over, and studied it like a puzzle box. It was round, papery, with a little tuft sticking out of the top and a root end poking out the bottom.

Nora took it back and frowned at it. The rolling happened because the thing was round, but she couldn't exactly flatten it by wishing. Then she noticed something. The onion wasn't a ball, really. It had a top and a root, two ends, and the roundness bulged out between them. If she cut it in half from top to root, she'd get two pieces with flat cut sides and rounded backs. She turned the knife the long way, set the onion on the board, and pressed down through the tuft to the root. It split with a soft snap, and she laid each half flat side down.

"Whoa," Kelly-Anne said. "It's just sitting there."

Nora nudged one half with the knife handle. It didn't move. She tilted the wobbly table on purpose, and still it stayed put. A flat face on the board meant no rolling, even on a table that behaved like a seesaw. She felt like she'd discovered a secret rule of the universe, and maybe she had, at least the onion part.

"Curved fingers, knuckles forward, thumb behind," she told herself, curling her left hand into a claw over the half onion so the blade rode against her knuckles and nowhere near her fingertips. The first slice came out a little thick. The second was better. By the fourth she had a rhythm going, and little half-moons of onion piled up on the board.

Mr. Foster strolled over with the pot and peered into it. "That's a proper claw grip," he said. "And you halved it before slicing. Smart."

"I had to," Nora said. "It kept escaping." She scraped the onions into the hot oil, and they hit the pan with a hiss that made all three of them cheer.

"Add the tomatoes," Ayla said, sliding the bowl over. "And don't forget, no cheese on Kelly-Anne's plate. She told me her allergy is why she eats crackers like a squirrel."

"It's a real allergy," Kelly-Anne protested, laughing. "Squirrels are just cautious."

Nora stirred the sauce and watched it bubble, tasting a spoonful to evaluate whether it needed more garlic. It did. She added it, and the smell that rose up made even the squirrel joke stop.

"First pick of pasta," Kelly-Anne said, holding up a fork in salute.

"First pick," Nora said, and lifted the pot off the fire.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
Nicholas stood in the lunch line on Thursday and discovered that the last chocolate chip muffin now cost two dollars instead of one. He counted his money twice. Two dollars meant no juice, and he wanted both.

"Ridiculous," said Jonas behind him. "Ms. Bianchi can't just raise the price. The person buying should decide what something costs."

"Wrong," said Samar, who was holding exactly one dollar and looking miserable. "She owns the muffins. The seller decides."

They argued all the way to the cash register, and Nicholas bought the muffin and nothing else, chewing slowly to make it last. The next morning he watched the bakery cart arrive, and it was smaller than usual. The delivery driver shrugged and said something about the bakery's oven being broken, then rolled the cart away to transport the empty trays back to the kitchen.

By Monday the muffins were back, dozens of them, stacked in baskets. The price had dropped to seventy-five cents. Jonas bought three and lined them up on his tray like trophies, but Samar had spent his allowance at the arcade on Friday and could only stare at them.

"See?" Jonas said. "Now the seller lowered the price. So the seller decides."

"But she raised it when everyone wanted them," Samar said. "She only lowered it when nobody could get one and then there were too many."

Nicholas frowned. Something was wrong with the whole argument, and he could feel it the way you can feel a door sticking without seeing the bent hinge. Neither answer could be the whole answer, because the price had moved in both directions while Ms. Bianchi stayed exactly the same person.

At lunch he went to the library instead of the cafeteria and searched until he found an economics book with a chapter on Alfred Marshall. He read one paragraph twice, then carried it back to the cafeteria at a jog.

"Listen," he said, dropping into the seat across from Jonas and Samar. "In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price."

"So we were both right," Samar said slowly.

"And both wrong," Jonas said, and laughed.

Nicholas slid the book between them. Seventy-five cents was still in his pocket, but the last muffin in the basket had just been taken by a kid from the other line, and Ms. Bianchi was already penciling something new on the price card.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
The train rattled south toward the coast, and Arianna had the window seat, which she had won fairly by getting to the platform first. Across from her, Mathew was reading the same beach safety brochure for the fifth time. "It says this beach is notorious for rip currents," he said. "What even is that?"

"A current that pulls you out away from the beach," said Abrielle, who sat beside him peeling an orange. "My cousin got caught in one in Florida. She said it felt like the whole ocean was dragging her, and swimming back in did nothing."

Arianna frowned at the brochure. "So what are you supposed to do, just float to Portugal?"

"The sign at the lifeguard tower said to swim along the beach," Abrielle said. "Parallel. Out of the current, because it's narrow."

"That's backwards," Mathew said. "If the beach is that way, you swim that way."

Arianna turned the brochure sideways and studied the little diagram, the arrow pulling out and the narrow band it sat in. "Think about it. The current is like a river, and rivers are narrow. If you swim across the river instead of upstream, you get out fast. If you swim straight against it, you tire out before you reach the sand."

Mathew tapped his chin. "Okay, but how do we test it without, you know, drowning?"

The problem nagged at her through two tunnels and a snack cart. Their hotel had a lazy river, a slow loop of water that pushed swimmers around a circle. Her little brother, who was notorious in the family for refusing to hold the handrail, had already irritated the lifeguard twice that morning by climbing out mid-loop. On day two, Arianna stood at the edge of the lazy river and noticed the jets: two spots where the push was strongest, a narrow band of fast water between the calm sections.

"I'm testing something," she announced, and pushed off. When she hit the jet stream, she tried swimming straight against it, pushing hard. The water shoved her backward, and the effort made her arms burn. The lifeguard's whistle chirped once, probably suspecting her brother's genes. Then she stopped fighting, turned sideways, and swam across the narrow band. Four strokes, and she was through, floating in calm water on the other side.

"Okay," Mathew called from the edge, where he had come to watch. "Say it in words."

"Swim parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, not straight against it. Way easier." She said it to the lifeguard too, and to her brother, whose conscience finally made him listen after Abrielle explained that real rip currents were the ocean's version of his lazy river, but stronger.

On their last day, the ocean itself proved the point. Mathew waded out past his waist, felt the tug, panicked for exactly two seconds, then turned and swam along the shore until the pull vanished. He walked out of the surf grinning like he'd invented water.

"Parallel," he said, holding up a flat hand. "I want that on a T-shirt."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain.
story:
Cooper spread the graph paper across the library table and tried for the third time to draw the rainfall bars for his desert climate chart. The project was due first period tomorrow, and the library closed in forty minutes. Stella had already finished her rainforest poster, all fat blue bars stacked high on her page, and Calvin was halfway through his savanna graph, so Cooper was the one slowing the group down.

"Your desert looks wrong," Stella said, leaning over. "There's just nothing there. You can't hand in a graph with empty space."

Cooper pointed at the climate data sheet Ms. Hussain had printed for them. "That's what the numbers say. Almost no rain at all, every single month." He frowned at the row of zeros. Except zeros weren't quite right either. Some months didn't have numbers at all, just a small note beside the station name, and the note was the part he kept rereading. He flipped the sheet over, then back, as if the missing data might be concealing itself somewhere on the other side.

Calvin came around the table. "So draw tiny bars. Everyone knows deserts get a little rain."

"No," Cooper said slowly. He was chasing an idea now, and he could feel it forming. "What if the bars aren't missing because someone forgot them? What if there's nothing to record?" He grabbed his pencil and wrote a line under his empty graph: Parts of Chile's Atacama Desert are so dry that some weather stations there have never recorded rain. Then he added one flat line across the whole rainfall section and labeled it zero.

"Ms. Hussain will think you skipped it," Calvin warned.

So Cooper walked to the front desk, where Ms. Hussain was checking in a returns cart with quick, agile movements, flipping books into the bin without looking up. He laid his sheet in front of her. "Is this real? Stations with no rain, ever?"

She stopped, read the note, and smiled a little. "Never recorded rain. Some of them. That's what the sheet says."

He carried the sheet back like a prize. Stella looked at his flat line, then at her crowded blue bars, and laughed. "From my perspective, your desert is the most boring place on earth." But she got out her colored pencils anyway and helped him shade the temperature curve, hot and steady, while Calvin added a caption in his neat block letters. Ten minutes before closing, the poster was done, and it was good.

Walking out into the parking lot with the rolled poster under his arm, Cooper thought about those weather stations, standing year after year with nothing to write down. Somewhere in the world it had never once rained, and tomorrow his whole class would know it too, because of him. His bus pulled away from the curb, and he watched it go, and started the long walk home.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through an event, such as a settler's diary, while a secondary source is written later by someone studying it.
story:
Camille sat on the floor of her grandmother's attic, which smelled like cedar and old paper, holding her phone away from her ear. "Mr. Santoso says the essay needs a primary source," Tabitha said from the other end. "Not the textbook. I don't even know what that means." Camille scanned the boxes stacked under the round window. "I think it means something from the actual time," she said slowly. "Like, not written afterwards." There was a pause, and then Tabitha said, "Then what are we supposed to find, a time machine?" Camille laughed, but her eyes had already caught a leather book wedged between a hatbox and a stack of quilts.

The book was small enough to fit in one hand, and the cover had gone soft with age. Inside, in cramped brown ink, someone named Ruth Elkins had written about crossing the plains in a wagon. "June 14th. The corn in Illinois failed two years running, and Samuel says the land in Oregon is free to those who will work it. I confess I cried leaving my sister, but I could not watch the children go hungry another winter." Camille read it twice. Here it was, in one paragraph: the crops had failed, and the land out west was being given away. That was why people moved. Her textbook had said "economic reasons," which had always seemed like a fog to her, but Ruth Elkins made it a hungry winter and a crying sister.

Then Camille caught herself wondering something. How did she know the diary was real and not a copy some museum had printed? She formulated a quick test. She texted Alex a photo of the handwriting and asked, "Does this look like it was written with a ballpoint pen?" Alex wrote back within a minute: "No, the ink feathered into the paper. Ballpoint doesn't do that. Why?" Camille grinned. The ink had soaked and spread the way old ink did, which meant the words had been set down by a real hand, on the trail, by someone who lived through it. A textbook, she realized, was written much later by someone studying all of this, which made it a different kind of thing entirely.

She called Tabitha back. "A primary source is something made at the time by a person who lived through the event," Camille said, "like this settler's diary. A secondary source is written later by someone studying it. That's the textbook." Tabitha groaned with relief. "Then I'm coming over. My grandmother has a box of letters somewhere, and I want the good stuff for my essay too, not just you." Tabitha had been hoping all week to beat Camille's grade, and Camille knew it, which made her laugh instead of worry.

When Tabitha arrived, out of breath from the hill, Camille noticed something odd. One entry was written in pencil so neat it looked printed, unlike Ruth's spidery hand everywhere else. "Anomaly," Camille said, pointing at it. "Look, different writing." They decided it might have been added later by a family member, maybe Ruth's daughter finishing the last page, which meant even a primary source could hold a puzzle inside it. Camille put a sticky note there, a temporary marker until she could ask the county museum. "So the diary tells us why they went," Tabitha said, "and the strange page makes us want to know more." Camille turned back to the round window, holding the little book up to the light, and read the next line aloud.

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Each whole step on the pH scale is a tenfold change, so a solution at pH 3 is ten times more acidic than one at pH 4.
story:
Keira balanced the box of jars on one hip and elbowed the garage door open. The science fair started at nine tomorrow morning, and her project, twelve household liquids tested with litmus paper and a homemade pH chart, was still a mess of sticky labels and half-filled cups.

"Move your foot," said Karam, who was sprawled on the old couch with a pickle jar in one hand. "I'm doing the pickle juice."

"It dissolved part of a label already," Keira said. "Good sign." She tore a strip of blue litmus paper and dipped it in. It flared red instantly, so fast she almost missed it.

"pH 3," Karam read off the jar, holding up the chart where each color patch corresponded to a number. "And this soap water is pH 4. So the pickle juice is a tiny bit more acidic. One step."

Keira paused, her fingers still wet. Something about that didn't sit right. She dunked a fresh strip in the soap water, watched it turn pink but slower, softer. The pickle strip had gone red like it was angry.

"That's not how it works," she said slowly. "I read it in Ms. Liu's book. Each whole step on the scale is a tenfold change. The pickle juice is ten times more acidic than the soap water."

"Ten times?" Karam sat up so fast he knocked the jar against his knee and made a face like the tendon in his leg had personally betrayed him. "From one number?"

"Ten times. From pH 4 to pH 3."

"Prove it."

Keira looked around the garage. On the shelf sat her dad's old vinegar bottle and a jar of baking soda water she'd mixed an hour ago. She soaked two cotton balls, one in each, and held the vinegar one under the pickle strip and the baking soda one under the soap strip. The vinegar ball's smell punched through both. Then she dipped fresh paper in both liquids again, side by side, and set them on the workbench like two tiny flags.

"Look at how fast they change," she said. "The pickle strip doesn't hesitate. The soap one takes its time, like it's thinking about it."

Karam leaned in until his nose almost touched the paper. "Okay," he admitted. "Okay, that's a big difference. I'm rewriting my poster. Which says 'pH 3: slightly more acidic.' Which is now a lie I told to forty people."

They worked until the garage light buzzed overhead, relabeling every jar. When Joaquin biked over at eight to see the project, he read the poster aloud in a voice like a documentary narrator, which Karam declared "unusually eloquent for a guy who ate my sandwich yesterday."

At nine the next morning, the judge stopped at their table and tapped the pickle jar. "Tell me about this one."

Keira grinned and picked up the red strip, still flat and bright in its plastic sleeve. "Dip this in and find out," she said.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
story:
Autumn climbed out of the pool at the end of drills and felt worse than she had all season, even though the thermostat on the natatorium wall read only twenty-nine degrees. Last Saturday's game had been thirty-five degrees outside, and she had felt strong the whole four quarters. Today she could barely lift her arms for the last sprint, and Ian was hanging on the lane rope looking half asleep.

"That makes no sense," she told Rae in the changeroom, wringing out her cap. "It was way hotter last week."

Rae shrugged. "It's way stickier today. My towel won't even dry."

Autumn stopped with the towel in her hands. It was true. Last week, in the dry heat, her towel had gone stiff and dry before she'd finished changing. Today it hung damp and limp over her bag, and when she pressed her palm on the bench, the mark of her own sweat stayed there. Something about the stickiness, she thought. On dry days sweat must dry fast; on sticky days it just sits there. And if sweat was supposed to cool you somehow while it dried, then on a day like this nobody on the team was cooling properly, no matter how many water breaks they took.

"Question," she said to Mr. Malik before practice the next day, which was just as humid. "Last week it was hotter but drier, and we were all fine. Could the damp air be the problem? Like, the sweat can't dry, so it can't cool us, and we overheat?"

Mr. Malik rubbed his chin. "Try something and tell me what you find."

So she did. She soaked two small towels at the drinking fountain, hung one near the dehumidifier vent in the corner of the pool deck and one on the fence by the open door, and timed them with her watch. The one by the vent dried in under twenty minutes. The one by the door, where the air hung thick and steamy, stayed wet past the end of practice. It wasn't a formula she could write on paper, but it was evidence, and evidence was enough to act on.

At the next practice, which was muggier still, she raised her hand before warm-up. "Mr. Malik, it's really humid today. Sweat can't evaporate, so we'll overheat faster even though it's not that hot. Can we do shorter drills with more breaks in the shade?" Ian backed her up, saying he'd felt like a boiled potato all week, and even the quietest girl on the team nodded hard.

Mr. Malik split the session into rounds, with rest breaks under the awning where the air moved. In the water the game was as turbulent as always, bodies splashing and wheels turning, but when Autumn climbed out after the last drill, her legs still felt like legs. Ian participated in the cool-down relay for the first time all week, and Rae fanned herself with the towel that had finally, near the vent, gone dry.

"Same thing tomorrow," Mr. Malik said, squinting at the sky, where grey clouds were stacking up for more rain. "Think it'll be even muggier?"

Autumn grinned and picked up her damp cap. "Guess we'll find out."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
The message hit the group chat at 9:47 p.m., when Joshua was supposed to be finishing his math homework. Hasan had posted a screenshot of a page titled "Joshua's Totally Awesome Blog," covered in bright green text and written by a version of Joshua who was eleven and thought fart jokes deserved paragraphs. Below it Hasan wrote, "WHERE has this been all my life," followed by three crying-laughing faces.

Joshua stared at the screenshot, and a memory rose up with the slow, ominous feeling of a door creaking open: sixth grade, the basement computer, his dad saying he could have a blog if he promised to be sensible about it. He had posted exactly four times before he got bored and forgot the password. He had assumed, the way you assume a dropped ice cream cone simply stops existing, that the blog had vanished with his interest in it.

He typed back, "I deleted it years ago." Hasan answered with a link. "Deleting only removes the original," Eleanor wrote a minute later, when Joshua asked how a dead page could still load. "Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone can look at old versions of lots of sites." She added, "It's called the Wayback Machine," like she was naming a band she liked. Then, before Joshua could even be embarrassed properly, she sent a second message: "Actually this is PERFECT. The school newspaper site from when my sister was editor got taken down, and I want those old issues for my history project. Can you help me find them?"

So Joshua tested it. He opened the archive site, pasted the newspaper's old address into the search bar, and held his breath. A timeline appeared, a row of dates like snapshots in an album. He clicked one, and the old front page bloomed onto his screen, banners and headlines and his sister's-friend's byline intact, whole issues there to categorize by year. Eleanor sent a row of exclamation points. "You're my ambassador to the ancient internet," she wrote. "Do you accept?"

He accepted. In the group chat they spent an hour pulling up issues from 2013, and Eleanor copied the links into a document for her project, thrilled, already drafting her introduction. The gain was real; so was the cost. Because when Joshua pasted in his own blog's address, just to check, the timeline filled in dates there too. Four posts, green text and all, saved and shareable by anyone, forever as far as he could tell. He deleted the message he'd started typing to Hasan, the one that said "not funny anymore, delete it." It wouldn't help, and he knew it.

He set the phone face-down on his desk, picked up his pencil, and got through two more math problems before the screen lit up again with Eleanor's name. "Found the issue where the gym flooded," she wrote. "Front page photo of a trash can floating. You're in the background, holding a mop."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
story:
Blake set the old wooden table in the middle of the backyard and weighed its corners with four smooth stones from the flowerbed. He was painting a color wheel for Mr. Nur, who had admired the idea at the school art show and asked for one to hang on his porch. Blake had drawn twelve wedges in pencil and filled in red, orange, and yellow before he noticed the problem: he had no idea who had thought of putting colors in a circle in the first place.

Kyla arrived on her bike with a bag of brushes, since Blake had used up his own good ones on the yellow. "Maybe some painter did it," she said, squeezing out a ribbon of green. "Like whoever invented the rainbow." Blake frowned at that. Rainbows were old, but circles felt like a decision somebody had made, and he wanted to get it right. He tried coordinate the wedges so opposite colors sat across from each other, red facing green, orange facing blue, and he tested it by spinning the board slowly on the table. When the pairs lined up, they seemed to argue with each other, which felt like proof the arrangement meant something.

The suspense came from the sky. Gray clouds had been stacking up over the fence since noon, and Blake worked faster, dabbing blue into its wedge while Kyla mixed purple with the last of the red. A fat drop hit the far corner of the board and diluted the orange into pale peach. Blake grabbed a cloth, but rubbing it was in vain; the blotch spread, and now the wheel looked lopsided, one wedge washed out like a color half remembered.

"Blake," a voice called from the next yard. Mr. Nur stood at the fence, holding a book with a cracked spine. He passed it over, opened to a marked page. "Isaac Newton, in his book Opticks, first published in 1704. He arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel." Blake turned the page and saw the circle of colors drawn centuries ago, the same shape sitting on his table.

"It was a scientist," Blake said. "Not a painter." Kyla leaned over the old diagram, forgetting the storm for a moment. Mr. Nur tapped the peach blotch on Blake's board with one finger.

"That one's mine," he said. "Leave it exactly as it is." The first heavy drops began to fall on the book's cover, and Blake pulled it under his shirt.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
story:
Jeremy slid into the back seat of the family car with his tie stuffed in his pocket, because he planned to put it on in the parking lot where nobody could watch him fumble. Loick climbed in beside him, and Mom pulled away from the curb before either of them had finished buckling.

"So what's the strategy?" Loick asked. "You've got a strategy, right? You always have a strategy."

"The speakers," Jeremy said. "The DJ booth is in the corner of the gym. If we stand right next to the speakers, everyone can see us, and it looks like we're not scared of anything." He had worked this out over three days of staring at the gym during lunch, mapping where the lights hung and where the crowd would thicken.

Mom glanced in the mirror. "Corner by the speakers. Bold choice." She did not say anything else, which Jeremy took as permission.

The dance was louder than he had imagined. He and Loick planted themselves by the right-hand speaker stack and stayed there through a whole hour, close enough that the bass pushed against his chest like a hand. When Derek arrived with a date, Jeremy did the vigorous, arm-swinging dance he had practiced in his room, and Derek nodded at him, actually nodded, and Jeremy decided the plan had worked perfectly. His ears felt strange when they left, kind of padded, like they were packed with cotton.

At two in the morning he woke up and lay very still, listening. There was a thin, high ringing in both ears, a steady note that did not come from anywhere in the house. He got up, checked the hallway, checked his phone. Nothing. The ringing was inside his ears, and it was still there when he woke again at eight.

He texted Loick. "Are your ears ringing?"

"YES. My mom says it has a name. She says it's called tinnitus. She says it means the music was loud enough to hurt your hearing and it's a warning sign."

Jeremy sat on the edge of his bed and thought about that for a while. A warning sign meant something had already gone wrong, or almost. He had treated the ringing like it was proof of a good night, a badge, and instead it was the opposite. His plan had worked for looking brave and failed for everything else, so he revised it: same corner, same dancing, twice the distance.

At school on Monday he found Derek at the water fountain. "Next dance, we're setting up ten feet back from the booth," Jeremy said. "That's where the sound is still huge but your ears don't pay for it."

Derek squinted at him. "Ten feet. You measured?"

"I paced it out this morning."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: In James Hurst's 1960 story The Scarlet Ibis, a storm-blown red bird dies in the family garden, foreshadowing the fate of the fragile boy Doodle.
story:
Luca spread the photocopy across the kitchen table and read the same page for the third time. Mr. Xu had assigned The Scarlet Ibis, a 1960 story by James Hurst, and had told the class only one thing before the bell rang: "Nothing in a good story is arbitrary." That word sat in Luca's notebook, circled twice.

A red bird blew into the story in a storm. It landed in the family garden, exhausted and far from home, and then it died. Luca flipped the page and stopped. Why would the writer spend a whole page on a bird that never came back? He texted Cecilia, who was reading the same story two streets away.

"Did the bird part feel weird to you?" he typed. "Like it meant something?"

Her reply came fast. "It's just a bird. A distraction maybe. My sister says the antagonist is the older brother, so the bird can't matter."

Luca frowned at the screen. "The brother is the antagonist, sure, but that doesn't exclude the bird from meaning something." He set the phone down and tried an experiment. He wrote BIRD in one column and DOODLE in the other. The bird was red. Doodle had been born with a red, shriveled body, so fragile everyone thought he would die. The bird was storm-blown, far from where it belonged. Doodle was fragile, different, struggling to keep up. Line by line, the two columns matched.

He called her. "The bird is a warning," he said. "Everything that happens to it, I think it happens to Doodle. It foreshadows him."

"Foreshadows?" Cecilia sounded skeptical. "You're guessing."

"I'm testing it. Watch." Luca read on, out loud over the phone, and slowed down when he reached the last pages. A storm came. Doodle, worn out and far behind his brother, fell in the wild field behind the house. Luca's voice got quieter as he read the final lines, and then he stopped and could not read any more, because Doodle was dead, and the older brother was kneeling beside a small, broken body under the red night sky.

Neither of them said anything for a moment. Rain started ticking against Luca's window, the same ordinary rain as any other night, except now it didn't feel ordinary at all.

"The garden," Cecilia said at last. "The bird died in the garden, and it was red, and Doodle..." Her voice trailed off.

"Same storm, same color, same ending," Luca said. "Mr. Xu is going to lose his mind when I show him my columns."

"Show me first," Cecilia said. "I'm coming over."

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: Many of the world's hot deserts lie near 30 degrees north or south of the equator, where sinking air warms up and dries out.
story:
The trail above the ranger station was dusty and smelled like baked sage, which Henry decided was appropriate, since his whole science project was about deserts. He sat on a flat rock and spread out the two graphs Ms. Whitaker had printed for him. One depicted the rainfall and temperature of the Sonoran Desert, all flat sad lines for precipitation and a temperature line that climbed like a startled cat. The other showed a rainforest, where the precipitation bars stacked so high they nearly ran off the page. Skylar flopped down beside him and peered at the papers.

"Yours got rained on," she said, pointing at the rainforest graph. "Mine just got sad on."

"That's the problem," Henry said. "I have to explain why they're different, and I keep getting it wrong." He thought about the day before, when he had told the class that deserts were hot because they were close to the equator, and Maximiliano had raised his hand and said, "Then why isn't the rainforest a desert? It's on the equator too." Henry had gone red and said something about the sun, which had been so vague it embarrassed him even as he said it. He turned that moment over now the way you tongued a sore tooth.

He unzipped his pack and pulled out the small globe Ms. Whitaker lent him, mostly so he could stop thinking about that classroom moment. The trail wind nudged the graph paper and he pinned it with a water bottle. He spun the globe slowly, and there it was. He tilted it toward the sun and traced with one finger. The Sahara. Then, crossing the equator through the green blot of the Congo and the Amazon, more deserts: the Kalahari, the Australian outback, the Atacama. He sat very still.

"Skylar. Look." He held up the globe. "The big deserts aren't on the equator. They line up in two belts, about thirty degrees north and south of it. That's where the air sinks, and it warms up and dries out as it comes down. So the equator gets the rain, and the belts get nothing." He tapped the Sahara, then the Atacama, then the Kalahari, one after another, like ringing three doorbells in a row.

"So your answer yesterday was backwards," Skylar said, grinning.

"Completely backwards." He laughed and pulled out his notebook, then hesitated. He could write the whole thing out neat and pretend he'd known it all along, or he could start with the moment Maximiliano caught him. The choice sat there, ambiguous for a second, and then he wrote at the top: First I got it wrong. He underlined it twice. "Next time Maximiliano asks a question, I'm bringing a globe," he said, and packed up the rock dust, the papers, and the last of his pride, and they hiked down toward the water fountain.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, range(2, n) produces the numbers from 2 up to n minus 1, so it tries every possible divisor except 1 and n itself.
story:
Jacob typed his program into the computer lab terminal, hoping this time it would finally work. The assignment from Ms. Guo was to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. On the whiteboard she had written a hint about using a loop to test divisors, then she had gone to help Jakub, whose screen had gone dark for the third time that period.

Jacob's idea was simple. Ask for a number, then check every possible divisor with a loop, and if any of them divided evenly, the number was not prime. He ran the program and typed in 7. NOT PRIME, the screen said. He frowned and tried 11. NOT PRIME. He tried 5, and 13, and even 2, the smallest prime of all. Every single answer came back the same.

"Try 4," said Bethany, leaning over from the next computer. "If it says not prime for that, at least it's right once." Jacob typed 4 and the program printed NOT PRIME again. Bethany laughed, but Jacob didn't. Something invisible was going wrong inside his code, some hidden cause he couldn't see on the screen.

He checked his if statement, his equals signs, his indentation. Then he slowed down and read the loop line one word at a time. "for i in range(2, n)," he said quietly. Bethany squinted at it. "What does that actually give you?" she asked. Jacob opened a second file and made the computer print what range(2, n) produced. For n equal to 7, it printed 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Not 7 itself. The loop was trying every possible divisor except 1 and n itself, which meant his code never tested n against n.

"That's the bug," Jacob said. Somewhere in his program, after the loop finished, his logic decided the number must not be prime. He didn't need to test n against n at all; he just needed to fix what happened after the checking was done. He deleted two lines, retyped the ending, and saved.

Ms. Guo passed behind them just as Jacob ran it again. He typed 7 and held his breath while the cursor blinked. The rain outside beat against the lab windows like a small monsoon, as if the weather itself were waiting. PRIME, the screen said. Jacob tried 9, and it said NOT PRIME, which was also correct. He tried 13, and it said PRIME again. Bethany raised her hand toward the ceiling. "Best output of the day," she said, and Jacob grinned and typed in 97 just to watch it one more time.
